25:9.prayer: Lord, everything I treasure is temporary apart from You. Loosen my grip on possessions, reputation, and comfort. Anchor my security in You alone, the God whose purposes stand forever. In Jesus' name, Amen.

25:10.devotion: God declares that the territory of Ammon and Moab would be given to the men of the East, and Ammon would not be remembered among the nations. This is sobering ancient narrative of judgment—God's word concerning nations that gloated over Judah's ruin proved true.
25:10.reflection: What legacy do I want to leave—will my life be remembered for pride or for faithfulness to God?
25:10.action: Do one small, unselfish act today that no one will notice—something done purely for God's eyes.
25:10.prayer: Father, my days are in Your hands. Help me live so that my life points others to You, not to my own ambitions. Keep me humble and faithful until the end. In Jesus' name, Amen.

25:11.devotion: God says He will execute judgments on Moab, and the result is repeated: they shall know that I am the LORD. This refrain runs through Ezekiel's oracles. Judgment, though severe, served God's greater purpose of revealing His identity to people who had ignored or dismissed Him.
25:11.reflection: Am I learning to know the Lord as He reveals Himself, or do I only turn to Him in hard times?
25:11.action: Read one psalm slowly today, noticing what it teaches about God's character, and note one insight.
25:11.prayer: Lord, You desire to be known truly by all people. Open my eyes to who You are each day—not only in trials but in quiet mercies. Make knowing You my deepest pursuit. Amen.

25:12.devotion: Edom's sin was vengeance—taking revenge on Judah when judgment had already fallen. Vengeance belongs to God, not to us. Edom added offense upon offense by seizing what it saw as a chance to settle old scores. The Lord confronts this grasping after justice that belongs to Him alone.
25:12.reflection: Am I holding a grudge and quietly hoping someone gets what they deserve?
25:12.action: Name one grudge you carry, and pray a blessing over that person today, entrusting the matter to God.
25:12.prayer: Father, You alone are the righteous Judge. I release my grievances to You. Free me from the weight of vengeance, and fill my heart with forgiveness as You have forgiven me in Christ. Amen.

25:13.devotion: Because Edom pursued revenge, God announces that His hand would be stretched out against it, bringing desolation from Teman, with Dedan falling by the sword. This is ancient prophetic judgment against a nation, not a model for personal action. It reminds us that settling scores is God's work, not ours.
25:13.reflection: How would my daily life change if I genuinely believed God will make all things right in His time?
25:13.action: When someone wrongs you today, pause and silently hand the situation to God before responding.
25:13.prayer: Lord GOD, I trust Your justice over my own instincts. Keep me from retaliation and from nursing wrongs. Help me respond to offenses with grace while leaving judgment in Your faithful hands. Amen.

25:14.devotion: Edom had treated Israel as an enemy when Jerusalem fell, rejoicing over their kin's disaster. God announces that judgment on Edom will come through Israel's hand, so that all parties recognize the LORD as the one who governs justice. In this prophetic oracle, God declares His commitment to holding nations accountable for cruelty.
25:14.reflection: When I am tempted to gloat over someone else's misfortune, how does God's view of such attitudes challenge me?
25:14.action: If you have secretly enjoyed a rival's setback this week, confess it to God today and pray one blessing over that person.
25:14.prayer: Righteous Lord, guard my heart from gloating and old grudges. Teach me to leave justice in Your hands, trusting Your wisdom and timing. Make me an instrument of mercy rather than spite, and let my life honor You today. In Jesus' name, amen.

25:15.devotion: God now turns to the Philistines, an ancient enemy of Israel. Their sin was vengeance carried out with a spiteful heart, rooted in enduring hatred, aiming at destruction. This verse names the motive God judges: not merely actions, but the bitterness driving them. Scripture shows God takes seriously the hidden posture of the heart.
25:15.reflection: What old hatreds or resentments are still living in my heart, quietly shaping how I treat others?
25:15.action: Name one lingering resentment in prayer today, then take one step toward release, such as writing it down and surrendering it to God.
25:15.prayer: Father, You see the hidden places of my heart. Where spite has taken root, pull it out and plant forgiveness there. Free me from the weight of old hatred, and help me love people the way You have loved me. Through Christ, amen.

25:16.devotion: Continuing the oracle against Philistia, God declares He will stretch out His hand against them and bring judgment on their coastal cities, including the Cherethites. Within Ezekiel's oracles against the nations, this passage assures God's people that no enemy nation escapes His notice. His justice is universal, not limited to one border or people.
25:16.reflection: Do I truly believe God sees every wrong, or do I feel pressured to arrange payback myself?
25:16.action: Choose one situation where you feel wronged and, instead of plotting a response, pray today entrusting that situation to God's just care.
25:16.prayer: Lord God, Your justice reaches everywhere, and nothing done in darkness escapes Your sight. Help me trust You with the wrongs I cannot fix. Keep my hands from vengeance and my heart at rest, knowing You are perfectly good and just. Amen.

25:17.devotion: This closing verse of the Philistine oracle repeats the word vengeance four times, underscoring that judgment belongs to God alone. The stated purpose is knowledge of the LORD—He acts so that nations, even hostile ones, will recognize who He is. These are prophetic words of ancient national judgment, revealing God's holy opposition to cruel vengeance.
25:17.reflection: How does knowing that vengeance belongs to the Lord free me from carrying burdens He never asked me to carry?
25:17.action: Memorize a brief reminder such as 'vengeance is Mine, says the Lord,' and repeat it whenever anger surfaces today.
25:17.prayer: Sovereign Lord, You alone execute perfect justice with perfect knowledge. I release my desire for revenge into Your hands. Let me live as one who trusts You, responding to wrongs with patience, prayer, and grace, until all things are made right by You. Amen.

26:1.devotion: This verse marks a date—precisely the eleventh year—when God's word came to Ezekiel again. The timestamp falls near Jerusalem's fall, a sober season for the exiles. It reminds readers that God kept speaking through His prophet even in the darkest days, and that His word arrives with real timing into real history.
26:1.reflection: In my own dark seasons, am I still listening for God's word, or have I assumed He has gone silent?
26:1.action: Set aside ten minutes today to read Scripture slowly, asking God to speak into your current season specifically.
26:1.prayer: Faithful God, thank You that Your word came in the darkest days of Your people's history. Speak into my season now. Give me ears to hear, patience to wait, and confidence that You are not silent. Anchor me in Your Word today. In Jesus' name, amen.

26:2.devotion: Tyre, a wealthy trading city, celebrated Jerusalem's fall, calling her the broken gateway of the peoples and expecting profit from her ruin. God hears this opportunistic rejoicing. The verse exposes a sin often overlooked: exploiting another's catastrophe for gain and satisfaction. Ancient Tyre's words become a warning against every heart that profits from others' pain.
26:2.reflection: Have I ever benefited financially, socially, or emotionally from someone else's misfortune without a thought for their suffering?
26:2.action: Examine one gain or advantage connected to another person's loss today, and if a repair or apology is needed, take the first step.
26:2.prayer: Lord, search my heart for the coldness Tyre showed. Forgive me for moments I ignored others' pain for my own benefit. Give me compassion that rejoices with those who rejoice and weeps with those who weep. Make my gains honest and my heart tender. Amen.

26:3.devotion: Because of Tyre's taunt, God declares Himself against her, promising that many nations will surge against the city like waves of the sea. In this prophetic judgment oracle, the imagery is striking: the power that made Tyre rich by sea traffic will become the picture of her undoing. God personally opposes the pride that mocks the fallen.
26:3.reflection: Where does pride or mockery have a foothold in my speech or attitudes, and what would it look like to surrender it?
26:3.action: Catch one mocking or superior comment before you say it today, and replace it with a kind or silent response.
26:3.prayer: God of all nations, You resist the proud but give grace to the humble. Strip away any contempt in my heart toward those who stumble. Clothe me in humility, guard my tongue, and let my words build up rather than tear down. In Christ, amen.

26:4.devotion: The oracle describes Tyre's destruction in vivid terms: walls destroyed, towers broken, the very dust scraped away until the city lies bare like the top of a rock. This is ancient prophecy of national judgment, showing that what human pride built on wealth and location could not withstand God's word. Security apart from God proves fragile.
26:4.reflection: What am I building my security on, and would it survive if God allowed it to be stripped away?
26:4.action: List your top three sources of security today, and pray over each one, consciously entrusting it to God rather than resting your hope on it.
26:4.prayer: Father, Tyre trusted walls, towers, and trade, and all of it crumbled. Show me the false securities I lean on. Build my confidence on You alone, the unshakable foundation. Whatever shakes around me, let my soul rest steady in Your faithfulness. In Jesus' name, amen.

26:5.devotion: Ezekiel pronounces God's judgment on Tyre, a wealthy coastal trading city that celebrated Jerusalem's fall. The Lord declares that this proud commercial hub will become a bare fishing spot in the sea, emptied of its splendor. The word of God, once spoken, cannot be undone.
26:5.reflection: Where might pride in my own success be quietly crowding God out of my life?
26:5.action: Identify one area of achievement you tend to take credit for, and today intentionally thank God for it in prayer.
26:5.prayer: Lord God, Your word stands when human empires fall. Humble my heart where pride has taken root. Teach me to hold my blessings loosely and to honor You as the true source of every good thing. Amen.

26:6.devotion: God's judgment on Tyre extends to her surrounding villages, her daughters in the fields. Even Tyre's dependencies and allies would share her fate. The purpose stated is sobering: that all would know the Lord. God's justice reaches every place human pride has spread.
26:6.reflection: Am I honest with myself that my choices affect the people connected to me?
26:6.action: Consider one person affected by your daily decisions, and today speak or act toward them with extra kindness and accountability.
26:6.prayer: Father, You see every corner of my life, even the places I forget. Help me live so that those around me see Your faithfulness, not just my failures. Make my whole life a witness that points to You. Amen.

26:7.devotion: God names His instrument of judgment: Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, arriving with horses, chariots, and a vast army. Ezekiel speaks this word to exiles who could hardly imagine such power shifting. Yet God rules over nations and empires, directing history according to His purposes.
26:7.reflection: When world events frighten or confuse me, do I remember that God remains sovereign over it all?
26:7.action: Today, read or watch the news briefly and then pray over one troubling headline, entrusting it to God's sovereign care.
26:7.prayer: Sovereign Lord, You raise up and bring down rulers and nations. When headlines overwhelm me, anchor my heart in Your unshakable throne. Grant wisdom to leaders and peace to all who feel powerless. I trust Your purposes. Amen.

26:8.devotion: The prophecy describes the siege in concrete detail: villages struck, siege mounds heaped, walls and defenses built against Tyre. God's word through Ezekiel was specific, not vague. Judgment was coming exactly as foretold, because Tyre's pride had defied both God and His people.
26:8.reflection: Do I take God's warnings in Scripture seriously, or do I assume they will never apply to me?
26:8.action: Choose one sin you have been excusing, and today take a first concrete step to confess it and change, perhaps by telling a trusted friend.
26:8.prayer: Gracious Father, thank You that Your warnings are gifts of mercy meant to turn me back. Give me a soft heart instead of a stubborn one. Convict me gently, correct me kindly, and keep me close to You. Amen.

26:9.devotion: Battering rams against walls and axes against towers: Ezekiel paints the machinery of ancient siege warfare dismantling Tyre's fortifications. Her defenses, impressive to human eyes, would prove no match. What people trust for security, apart from God, ultimately cannot stand when tested.
26:9.reflection: What am I leaning on for security, and would it survive if everything else was stripped away?
26:9.action: Write down one thing besides God that gives you a sense of safety, and today pray specifically, surrendering that reliance to Him.
26:9.prayer: Lord, I confess I often build walls of money, routines, and plans and call them security. Remind me that You alone are my fortress. Strengthen my trust in You, especially when the things around me feel uncertain. Amen.

26:10.devotion: The imagery intensifies: dust from countless horses covering the city, walls shaking at the rumble of chariots, gates breached like a conquered town. Ezekiel's hearers would feel the terror in these words. This was ancient war prophecy, describing how Tyre's confidence would crumble before God's declared judgment.
26:10.reflection: How do I respond when the foundations I assumed were stable begin to shake?
26:10.action: Memorize or write out one short verse about God's steadiness today, and recite it whenever you feel unsettled.
26:10.prayer: Father of peace, when my world trembles and everything feels loud and frightening, be my calm center. You have never abandoned those who trust You. Steady my heart today with Your presence and Your unchanging promises. Amen.

26:11.devotion: The prophecy continues with vivid pictures of conquest: streets trampled, people slain, and Tyre's strong pillars falling to the ground. The pillars symbolized civic pride and permanence, yet they would topple. Ezekiel speaks as a watchman warning of what God had declared, so hearers might heed the truth.
26:11.reflection: If something I have built my identity on fell tomorrow, what would still be standing in my life?
26:11.action: Name one pillar of your identity, such as work or reputation, and today do one act of service that no one will notice or praise.
26:11.prayer: Lord Jesus, You are the foundation that never falls. Loosen my grip on titles, reputations, and achievements. Build my life on things that last, and help me value faithfulness to You above every visible success. Amen.

26:12.devotion: The oracle closes with complete loss: riches plundered, merchandise taken, pleasant houses destroyed, and Tyre's very stones and timber cast into the water. The city famous for trade would lose everything it gained. Ezekiel's message warns that wealth accumulated without regard for God cannot be held forever.
26:12.reflection: Am I treating my possessions and earnings as a trust from God or as treasures to cling to?
26:12.action: Find one item or amount of money you can give away today, and do it quietly to meet someone's real need.
26:12.prayer: Generous God, everything I own came from Your hand. Forgive my hoarding and my anxiety over losing things. Make me a joyful steward who gives freely, holds lightly, and stores treasure in heaven with You. Amen.

26:13.devotion: In this oracle against Tyre, a wealthy merchant city famous for commerce and celebration, God announces judgment on its pride. The songs and harps that filled its streets will fall silent, a picture of how everything Tyre trusted for joy was about to be taken away.
26:13.reflection: What am I building my joy on that could not survive God's refining hand?
26:13.action: Name one source of comfort you rely on besides God, and thank Him today for being your deepest, most lasting joy.
26:13.prayer: Lord, silence the false songs in my life that drown out Your voice. Tune my heart to rejoice in You alone, so my gladness rests not on circumstances but on Your faithful love. Amen.

26:14.devotion: God declares that Tyre will become a bare rock where fishermen spread nets, never rebuilt to her former glory. The city that seemed untouchable would be laid bare. The reason given is weighty: the Lord Himself has spoken, and His word settles the matter.
26:14.reflection: Where do I act as though my life's structures are too solid ever to be torn down?
26:14.action: Write down one thing you consider secure, and pray over it, deliberately placing it in God's hands rather than your own.
26:14.prayer: Father, I confess I often trust what I can see and build. Teach me that only Your word stands forever. Anchor my security not in my achievements but in You, the Lord who has spoken. Amen.

26:15.devotion: Tyre's fall would send shockwaves through the surrounding coastlands. Her collapse was so significant that whole regions would shake at the news. This verse reminds us that one nation's judgment rippled outward, affecting many who had depended on her power and prosperity.
26:15.reflection: When someone else falls, do I pause to consider what it reveals about the fragility of all human power?
26:15.action: When you hear of a leader or institution failing today, resist gossip or gloating and instead pray for all those affected.
26:15.prayer: Lord, keep me from pride when others stumble, for I am weak too. Let every example of human failure remind me to lean wholly on Your strength and mercy. Amen.

26:16.devotion: The princes of the sea would strip off their royal robes and sit trembling on the ground, astonished at Tyre's fall. Kings who once ruled with confidence would be reduced to dread. Her downfall humbled even those who thought themselves secure on their thrones.
26:16.reflection: Am I prepared to be humbled when I discover my confidence rested on shifting foundations?
26:16.action: Identify one place where you feel 'entitled' or secure by status, and perform one humble, unseen act of service today.
26:16.prayer: Father, strip away my pride gently before circumstances do it painfully. Clothe me not in trembling but in trust. Make me willing to sit low before You, knowing that humility leads to Your grace. Amen.

26:17.devotion: The sea princes would sing a lament over Tyre, mourning the renowned city of seafarers whose strength had dominated the waters. Their mourning is mixed with a sober acknowledgment that her power had also spread fear. Greatness built on intimidation ended in grief and silence.
26:17.reflection: Does my influence make others feel safe and blessed, or does it leave them anxious around me?
26:17.action: Ask one person today how your words and presence affect them, and listen without defending yourself.
26:17.prayer: Lord, use my life to bring courage and peace to others, not fear or pressure. May the story people tell about me point to Your kindness rather than my strength. Amen.

26:18.devotion: Tyre's departure stunned the coastlands, and they trembled on the day of her fall. The verse closes the lament begun by the sea rulers, emphasizing how her absence unsettled everyone who traded and prospered through her. Her fall left a vacuum that no one could fill.
26:18.reflection: If God removed what I lean on most, who around me would notice my faith by how I respond?
26:18.action: Practice one small act of contentment today, choosing gratitude when something you planned or depended on falls through.
26:18.prayer: Father, when the things I rely on slip away, let my heart not tremble like the coastlands but rest in You. You remain when everything else departs. Steady me today. Amen.

26:19.devotion: God announces that Tyre would become desolate like ancient uninhabited cities, with the deep and great waters covering her. The imagery evokes overwhelming chaos and total undoing. What had risen to prominence by the sea would be swallowed by the very element that made her rich.
26:19.reflection: What rising tide in my life, good or bad, am I forgetting is ultimately under God's sovereign hand?
26:19.action: Before bed tonight, review your day and consciously surrender to God each success and each setback you experienced.
26:19.prayer: Sovereign Lord, the waters rise and fall at Your command. I place my rising seasons and my overwhelming ones in Your hands, trusting that You rule over every depth that threatens to cover me. Amen.

26:20.devotion: The oracle ends with Tyre brought down to the Pit, dwelling in desolation, never again inhabited. Yet the verse closes with hope of another kind: God declares He will establish glory in the land of the living. Judgment on pride makes way for glory that belongs to the Lord alone.
26:20.reflection: Am I seeking to make my own name glorious, or longing for God's glory to be established where I live?
26:20.action: Choose one ordinary task today and do it quietly and well, asking God to be glorified rather than you.
26:20.prayer: God of glory, bring down every tower I build to myself. Establish Your glory in my home, my church, and my land of the living, and let my small life gladly serve that great purpose. Amen.

26:21.devotion: Ezekiel's prophecy against Tyre concludes with a solemn word: the proud island city famous for commerce and wealth would fall and never be rebuilt as it once was. God's judgment addresses pride and self-sufficiency, reminding every nation and heart that lasting security belongs to the Lord alone, not to prosperity or reputation.
26:21.reflection: Where am I quietly trusting in my own achievements or resources more than in God?
26:21.action: Identify one area of security you lean on besides God, and deliberately pray over it, surrendering it to Him today.
26:21.prayer: Lord, forgive me for the times I have leaned on my own strength and success. Teach me that You alone are my refuge. Keep my heart humble, anchored not in what I have built, but in Your faithful love. Amen.

27:1.devotion: This simple verse marks a turning point in Ezekiel's message. After pronouncing judgment on Tyre, the prophet receives the word of the LORD again. It reminds us that God continues speaking to His people, guiding His prophets through each stage of a long and difficult message, faithful to reveal His will step by step.
27:1.reflection: Am I listening expectantly for God's word, even when it comes in seasons I did not expect?
27:1.action: Set aside ten quiet minutes today to read Scripture slowly and listen, asking God to speak to your present situation.
27:1.prayer: Father, thank You that You are a God who still speaks through Your Word. Quiet my heart and sharpen my ears. Help me receive Your voice with humility today, trusting that Your word comes exactly when I need it. Amen.

27:2.devotion: God instructs Ezekiel to take up a lamentation for Tyre. Even in announcing judgment, the tone is mournful, not gleeful. Scripture models here a grief over lostness and downfall. It teaches God's people to view even deserved consequences with sorrow and compassion rather than triumph, remembering that God takes no pleasure in ruin.
27:2.reflection: When someone faces the consequences of pride or wrongdoing, do I respond with compassion or with satisfaction?
27:2.action: Pray today for someone who is experiencing hardship or trouble, asking God to bring them comfort, wisdom, and restoration.
27:2.prayer: Gracious God, soften my heart toward those who suffer, even when their troubles stem from their own choices. Give me Your compassion instead of judgment. Use me to bear others' burdens gently, reflecting Your mercy in a hard world. Amen.

27:3.devotion: Tyre sat advantageously at the entrance of the sea, a merchant to many coastlands, and its boast was 'I am perfect in beauty.' The city's self-description reveals the heart of the issue: pride in its position, beauty, and success. Ezekiel's lament exposes how easily blessing and prominence can become the ground of self-glorification rather than gratitude.
27:3.reflection: What gifts or advantages in my life have I begun to credit to myself rather than to God?
27:3.action: Write down three blessings you enjoy, and beside each one write a note of thanksgiving to God as its true source.
27:3.prayer: Lord, every good thing I have comes from Your hand. Guard me from the pride that says, 'I am perfect in beauty.' Cultivate in me a grateful, humble spirit that points others to You rather than to myself. Amen.

27:4.devotion: The lament pictures Tyre as a magnificent ship, its borders set in the midst of the seas, its builders perfecting its beauty. The imagery is striking: human skill and craftsmanship made the city splendid. Yet this very ship, so carefully constructed, was headed for shipwreck because of pride. Excellence is a gift, but it cannot secure a destiny apart from God.
27:4.reflection: Do I rely on my own craftsmanship and effort to guarantee my future, forgetting the One who holds it?
27:4.action: Before starting your main task today, briefly acknowledge God as the giver of your skills and commit your work's outcome to Him.
27:4.prayer: Father, thank You for skills, opportunities, and the work of my hands. Keep me from making my abilities an idol or my achievements an anchor. I entrust my efforts and my future to You, the true Builder of my life. Amen.

27:5.devotion: Ezekiel details Tyre's ship-like splendor: planks of fir from Senir, a mast of cedar from Lebanon. The best materials from distant places were gathered to build the city's glory. The description honors genuine craftsmanship while setting up the lament's deeper point: the most impressive vessel, stocked with the finest resources, cannot withstand God's judgment on pride.
27:5.reflection: What am I gathering to impress others, and would it still matter if God alone were my audience?
27:5.action: Choose one task today to do quietly and well, without seeking recognition, offering it to God as your audience.
27:5.prayer: Lord, You see the materials I gather and the image I try to build. Free me from the need to impress. Let my finest work be an offering to You, done faithfully whether or not anyone else notices. Amen.

27:6.devotion: The lament continues with oars of oak from Bashan and planks inlaid with ivory from Cyprus. Tyre's beauty was a global collaboration, drawing luxury from many nations. Ezekiel carefully catalogs this splendor, not to condemn beauty itself, but to show how thoroughly the city trusted in wealth and refinement. Such trust, Scripture warns, is a fragile foundation.
27:6.reflection: How much of my sense of worth rests on possessions or the quality of my lifestyle?
27:6.action: Thank God aloud for one non-material gift He has given you, such as a relationship, a calling, or His presence.
27:6.prayer: Generous God, thank You for the good things of life, including beauty and provision. Forgive me when I confuse luxury with worth. Root my identity in Your love, which no wealth can buy and no loss can take away. Amen.

27:7.devotion: Tyre's sail was fine embroidered linen from Egypt, its covering blue and purple from Elishah, colors associated with royalty and luxury. Ezekiel paints the city in the richest fabrics imaginable, a vessel dressed in splendor. Yet this adornment belonged to a ship destined for grief. Earthly magnificence, however dazzling, cannot shield a heart or a city from the truth of God's holiness.
27:7.reflection: If all my outward adornment were stripped away, what would remain as the true substance of my life?
27:7.action: Declutter one visible symbol of image-keeping this week, and give the time or money saved to someone in need.
27:7.prayer: Father of all beauty, You made color, fabric, and splendor for our joy. Keep these gifts from becoming my covering. Clothe me instead in Your righteousness and humility, so my life reflects Your glory and not merely my own display. Amen.

27:8.devotion: God speaks to Tyre through the prophet Ezekiel, picturing the city as a magnificent ship. Sidon and Arvad supplied the rowers, while Tyre's own wise men served as pilots. The image shows how Tyre gathered talent from many places, yet the picture builds toward a warning about pride in earthly greatness.
27:8.reflection: Whose wisdom am I trusting to steer the course of my life?
27:8.action: Identify one decision you're facing, and intentionally ask God for guidance before consulting any other source today.
27:8.prayer: Lord, You are wiser than every skilled advisor. Forgive me when I rely on my own cleverness or the world's expertise above You. Take the helm of my life and steer me in Your ways. In Jesus' name, Amen.

27:9.devotion: The ship of Tyre needed skilled craftsmen to keep it seaworthy. The elders of Gebal caulked its seams, and sailors from everywhere served its trade. Ezekiel describes the city's impressive network with admiration, yet within a lament that reminds hearers that no human enterprise, however impressive, can secure a nation's future.
27:9.reflection: Am I building my security on human networks or on God's faithfulness?
27:9.action: Thank one person whose behind-the-scenes faithfulness supports your life, and thank God for providing them.
27:9.prayer: Father, thank You for the many people whose quiet work sustains my life. Keep me from trusting systems and connections more than I trust You. You alone hold my seams tight when storms come. Amen.

27:10.devotion: Ezekiel's portrait of Tyre as a ship continues with its defenders. Soldiers from Persia, Lydia, and Libya served in its army, hanging shields and helmets that added splendor. The city looked glorious and well protected. Yet this chapter is a lament, teaching that military might and outward beauty cannot shield a people from God's judgment on pride.
27:10.reflection: What am I tempted to rely on for protection when I feel vulnerable?
27:10.action: Write down one area where you feel unprotected, then pray over it, entrusting it specifically to God today.
27:10.prayer: God of all refuge, forgive me for the times I lean on shields that cannot save. You are my fortress and my deliverer. Help me rest in Your protection rather than the outward strength of this world. Amen.

27:11.devotion: The picture of Tyre grows grander: men of Arvad and Gammad manned its walls and towers, their shields making its beauty complete. Ezekiel paints a city at the height of splendor. But the context is sorrowful, for God announced Tyre's fall. The verse reminds us that perfection in appearance is not the same as standing right with God.
27:11.reflection: Is my life more concerned with looking complete than with being faithful?
27:11.action: Choose one hidden area of your life today and tend to it honestly before God rather than polishing appearances.
27:11.prayer: Lord, You see beneath the surface of my life. Forgive me for valuing a polished image over a honest heart. Make me beautiful in Your sight through humility, truth, and faithfulness. In Jesus' name, Amen.

27:12.devotion: Tarshish traded with Tyre, exchanging silver, iron, tin, and lead for its luxury goods. Ezekiel catalogs Tyre's vast commerce to show how wealthy and admired the city had become. Yet the lament's purpose is sobering: abundance itself was never the problem; the pride and self-glorification that grew with it were what God judged.
27:12.reflection: Has God's provision in my life drawn me closer to Him or fed a sense of self-sufficiency?
27:12.action: List three material blessings you enjoy and thank God for each one aloud, acknowledging Him as their giver.
27:12.prayer: Father, every good gift comes from Your hand. Keep my heart soft as You provide, and guard me from the pride that wealth can quietly grow. Teach me to hold things loosely and hold You tightly. Amen.

27:13.devotion: Among Tyre's trading partners, Ezekiel names Javan, Tubal, and Meshech, who bartered human lives and bronze for merchandise. This sober detail acknowledges that Tyre's prosperity was entangled with trafficking in people. The passage stands as a witness that God sees how wealth is gained, and commerce built on exploiting human beings comes under His judgment.
27:13.reflection: Do my purchases and profits honor the dignity of every person involved?
27:13.action: Learn one fact today about ethical or fair-trade options for a product you buy, and consider switching to a more just source.
27:13.prayer: Lord, You made every person in Your image, and no profit justifies treating anyone as goods. Forgive Your people where we benefit from injustice unknowingly. Make us attentive, compassionate, and just in all our dealings. Amen.

27:14.devotion: Togarmah traded horses, steeds, and mules for Tyre's wares, adding livestock to the city's wide commercial reach. Ezekiel's catalogue shows a marketplace drawing goods from distant nations. The chapter's larger message remains: such reach and prosperity, while remarkable, became the object of Tyre's boasting, and boasting in abundance invited God's correction.
27:14.reflection: When I describe my blessings, do my words point to God's goodness or to my own success?
27:14.action: The next time you tell someone about a blessing, include how God provided it rather than only your own effort.
27:14.prayer: Generous God, thank You for the wide range of good things You place in my life. Keep boasting far from my lips. May my words about my blessings always give You credit and draw others to Your kindness. Amen.

27:15.devotion: The men of Dedan and many coastlands traded with Tyre, bringing ivory tusks and ebony. Even distant islands found their market in the city's commerce. Ezekiel paints Tyre as the hub of the known world's trade. Yet this climax of abundance sits inside a lament, reminding readers that earthly reach, however vast, cannot deliver a soul before God.
27:15.reflection: If my influence and resources were taken away tomorrow, would my faith remain standing?
27:15.action: Give away one item or resource today to someone in need, practicing holding possessions with an open hand.
27:15.prayer: Father, only You are my true security. If everything else were stripped away, let my hope rest unshaken in You. Teach me to use my resources generously while my grasp on them stays light. In Jesus' name, Amen.

27:16.devotion: In this lament over Tyre, Ezekiel pictures the city as a magnificent trading ship, and Syria appears among its business partners. Tyre's abundant goods drew nations from afar, exchanging emeralds, purple cloth, embroidery, fine linen, corals, and rubies. The prophet shows how far Tyre's wealth and influence reached, even as the poem moves toward mourning its coming downfall.
27:16.reflection: When God blesses the work of my hands, do I remember Him or begin to trust the abundance itself?
27:16.action: Take note today of one material blessing you enjoy, and thank God for it aloud before you use it.
27:16.prayer: Generous Father, every good gift comes from Your hand. Keep my heart from resting in treasures that fade. Teach me to hold Your blessings loosely and to honor You, the Giver, above all that I possess. Amen.

27:17.devotion: Among Tyre's many trading partners, Ezekiel lists Judah and Israel, who brought agricultural goods and products of the land: wheat from Minnith, millet, honey, oil, and balm. Even God's covenant people were woven into the region's economy. The verse reminds us that daily provisions like grain and honey mattered as much as jewels in the commerce of the ancient world.
27:17.reflection: Do I see ordinary work, trade, and daily bread as places where God is present and faithful?
27:17.action: Do one routine task today, such as shopping or cooking, consciously as an act of gratitude to God.
27:17.prayer: Lord of daily bread, thank You for the ordinary gifts that sustain life. Help me see Your faithfulness in routine work and simple meals. Keep me grateful in seasons of plenty and trusting in seasons of need. Amen.

27:18.devotion: Damascus joins the roster of Tyre's merchants, drawn by the city's many luxury items. Ezekiel names the famed wine of Helbon and white wool as goods that passed through these trade relationships. In the middle of the lament, the prophet catalogs these exchanges to show how extensive Tyre's glory was, preparing the reader to feel the weight of its loss.
27:18.reflection: Am I chasing the finest and rarest things, or am I learning contentment with what God provides?
27:18.action: Identify one want you have been treating as a need, and consciously release it to God in prayer today.
27:18.prayer: Father, forgive me when luxury and comfort quietly become my pursuit. Teach me contentment in every circumstance and a heart that treasures You above fine things. Order my desires so that I want what is truly good. Amen.

27:19.devotion: Dan and Javan appear in Ezekiel's list as traders who traveled back and forth to Tyre's markets, bringing wrought iron, cassia, and sweet cane. The picture is of steady movement and exchange, people making long journeys to do business. Ezekiel records this bustle to display the breadth of Tyre's commerce, even as the whole structure is heading toward sorrow and loss.
27:19.reflection: In the constant coming and going of my life, what am I actually traveling toward, and does it honor God?
27:19.action: Choose one journey or errand today to use deliberately for kindness, such as helping someone along the way.
27:19.prayer: Lord, my days are full of comings and goings. Direct my steps so that all my traveling serves Your purposes. Keep me from being so busy with trade and tasks that I forget You are the destination of my heart. Amen.

27:20.devotion: Dedan, a group known in the ancient Near East for desert trade routes, appears briefly in Ezekiel's catalog as Tyre's merchant in saddlecloths for riding. Even a short mention fits the prophet's larger design: naming partner after partner to show how many peoples had invested in Tyre's prosperity, and how widespread the grief would be when that prosperity fell.
27:20.reflection: When small or unglamorous parts of my work seem unnoticed, do I still offer them faithfully to God?
27:20.action: Do one small, easily overlooked task today with care, offering it quietly to God as service to Him.
27:20.prayer: Faithful God, You see the small work that no one else notices. Remind me that my worth is not in prominence but in serving You with what is in my hands today. Bless the humble tasks I offer to You. Amen.

27:21.devotion: Ezekiel names Arabia and the princes of Kedar as regular merchants with Tyre, trading in lambs, rams, and goats. Herders from the desert regions brought their livestock to the great market city. This mention shows that everyday goods, not only luxuries, flowed through Tyre, and that even leaders of distant peoples depended on its trade in the days before its lamented fall.
27:21.reflection: The traders offered what they actually had, from their own flocks; am I offering God what I truly have?
27:21.action: Offer God one real resource you possess today, such as time, a skill, or an item, by using it for someone else.
27:21.prayer: Shepherd of the flocks, You ask for what we truly have, not what we wish we had. Receive my ordinary offerings, and show me how my small provisions can serve others and glorify You today. Amen.

27:22.devotion: The merchants of Sheba and Raamah traded with Tyre, bringing the choicest spices, precious stones of every kind, and gold. Sheba was famed in Scripture for rich caravans, and here its finest goods feed Tyre's splendor. Ezekiel includes them in the roll call of partners whose commerce made the city gleam, just before the lament turns to its tragic end.
27:22.reflection: What is the most valuable thing in my life, and how would God know it by the way I treat it?
27:22.action: Give something of real value today, such as money or time, to a person or ministry in genuine need.
27:22.prayer: Lord of all gold and spice, every treasure traces back to You. Guard my heart from worshiping what glitters. Make me generous with the best I have, that others may see Your goodness through my giving. Amen.

27:23.devotion: Ezekiel closes this stretch of the merchant list with Haran, Canneh, Eden, the merchants of Sheba, Assyria, and Chilmad, all trading partners of Tyre. The names pile up like ledger entries, city after city bound to the great port's economy. The accumulation builds the scale of Tyre's reach, heightening the sorrow of the lament that announces its fall.
27:23.reflection: If others were asked what my life is built around, would their answer point to God or to something less?
27:23.action: Write down what your schedule and spending reveal you are building your life around, and pray over the list.
27:23.prayer: Sovereign God, You read the true ledger of my life. Where I have built around lesser things, forgive me and rebuild me on Christ, the sure foundation. Let my days be spent for Your kingdom and glory. Amen.

27:24.devotion: In this lament over Tyre, Ezekiel catalogs the luxury goods that flowed through the city's markets—purple cloth, embroidered garments, and woven cords. Tyre's wealth depended on trade partnerships with many nations. The passage reminds us how easily a city, or a heart, can rest its confidence in beautiful and costly things rather than in God.
27:24.reflection: Where am I tempted to find security in what I own rather than in God who provides?
27:24.action: Choose one possession you treasure and intentionally thank God for it today, acknowledging Him as its true source.
27:24.prayer: Lord, forgive me for the times I have trusted in possessions more than in You. Keep my heart anchored in Your goodness, and teach me to hold earthly things loosely, with gratitude and open hands. Amen.

27:25.devotion: Tyre sat at the height of its glory, its merchant ships carrying goods across the seas. The city seemed prosperous, filled, and magnificent. Ezekiel paints this picture deliberately, because the greater the splendor described, the more sobering the fall that follows. Earthly glory, however impressive, is never permanent.
27:25.reflection: When I look at seasons of success in my life, do I remember to give glory to God rather than to myself?
27:25.action: Write down three blessings in your life today and thank God for each one by name in prayer.
27:25.prayer: Father, every good thing I enjoy comes from Your hand. Guard me from pride when seasons go well, and help me remember that all glory belongs to You alone. Keep me humble and thankful. Amen.

27:26.devotion: The imagery shifts as the east wind breaks Tyre's ship in the midst of the seas. All the skilled rowing and navigation could not withstand the storm God sent in judgment. Human effort and expertise, however great, cannot save us when we stand against the Lord. This is ancient prophecy, yet it speaks to the limits of self-reliance.
27:26.reflection: In what area of my life am I relying on my own skill instead of seeking God's guidance?
27:26.action: Identify one decision you are facing and pause to pray about it before acting on it today.
27:26.prayer: Lord, You are stronger than every wind and wave. Forgive my self-reliance, and teach me to bring my plans before You first. Anchor my life in Your wisdom rather than my own strength. Amen.

27:27.devotion: Ezekiel lists everything and everyone that would sink with Tyre—riches, wares, sailors, pilots, craftsmen, and warriors. When judgment came, no rank or profession was spared, because the whole system rested on a corrupt foundation. The verse warns that a life built without God collapses entirely, taking everything with it.
27:27.reflection: If everything I have built were suddenly tested, what foundation would it prove to rest upon?
27:27.action: Spend ten minutes today examining one habit or plan, asking honestly whether it honors God or only serves yourself.
27:27.prayer: Search me, O God, and show me anything in my life built on sand. Give me courage to rebuild on Your Word, the only foundation that holds when everything else falls away. Amen.

27:28.devotion: The cry of Tyre's pilots was so great that even the mainland trembled at the sound. The sailors who once commanded the waters now shouted in despair as their city sank. Ezekiel shows that the fall of the proud sends ripples far beyond themselves; a nation's collapse touches many ordinary lives.
27:28.reflection: How do the choices I make today affect the people around me who depend on me?
27:28.action: Think of one person who relies on you, and do something concrete today to strengthen and encourage them.
27:28.prayer: Father, remind me that my life touches others in ways I rarely see. Help me live faithfully so that my influence brings blessing, not sorrow, to those who look to me. Amen.

27:29.devotion: Tyre's sailors and pilots abandoned their ships and stood helpless on the shore. The men who spent their lives on the sea could do nothing as the source of their livelihood and pride was destroyed. Ezekiel portrays the utter helplessness of those who trusted in a system God had appointed to fall.
27:29.reflection: What would I do if the source of my income or identity were suddenly taken away?
27:29.action: Name one earthly support you depend on, and pray specifically, entrusting it to God's care today.
27:29.prayer: Lord, You alone are my rock and refuge. If everything I depend on were stripped away, help me know that You remain. Teach me to rest my whole life in Your unchanging faithfulness. Amen.

27:30.devotion: The lament reaches its most vivid point: sailors weep bitterly, cast dust on their heads, and roll in ashes over Tyre's fall. These were ancient signs of deep mourning. Even Tyre's trading partners grieved, for her ruin touched them all. Ezekiel shows that sin's consequences bring sorrow that spreads far beyond the one who sinned.
27:30.reflection: When I witness loss or failure, do I respond with hardened indifference or with honest, compassionate grief?
27:30.action: Reach out today to someone who is grieving or struggling, offering a listening ear or a simple word of comfort.
27:30.prayer: Compassionate God, soften my heart toward those who suffer. Keep me from indifference, and make me willing to weep with those who weep, pointing them gently to Your comfort and hope. Amen.

27:31.devotion: Tyre's mourners shaved their heads, wore sackcloth, and wailed with bitterness of heart. The mourning was genuine and overwhelming, for the fall of so great a city stunned everyone who knew her. The passage closes the picture of Tyre's lament, leaving readers to consider how quickly splendor can become sorrow when a life is built apart from God.
27:31.reflection: What would true, honest repentance look like in my own life right now?
27:31.action: Set aside fifteen minutes today for honest prayer, confessing one specific sin and asking God for a changed heart.
27:31.prayer: Merciful Father, I do not want to mourn over ruins I built myself. Create in me a clean heart, and turn me back to You now, while grace is offered, so my life may rest in You. Amen.

27:32.devotion: Ezekiel's lament over Tyre pictures the shock of watching a great city fall. Sailors and traders who once celebrated Tyre now sing a funeral song, asking how something so impressive could be destroyed in the midst of the sea. The passage reminds us that no human achievement stands beyond God's judgment.
27:32.reflection: What am I tempted to believe is too strong or successful to ever fall?
27:32.action: Identify one thing you rely on besides God today, and deliberately place it in His hands through a short prayer of surrender.
27:32.prayer: Lord, You alone are unshakeable. Forgive me for trusting what looks permanent in this world. Teach me to build my hope on You, the only foundation that never falls. In Jesus' name, Amen.

27:33.devotion: Tyre's commerce blessed many nations. Her ships carried goods that satisfied people and enriched kings far and wide. Ezekiel acknowledges the city's genuine success before announcing its fall. Prosperity itself is not condemned here; the surrounding chapters show that Tyre's pride and self-exaltation were the problem.
27:33.reflection: When God blesses my work and it benefits others, do I give Him the credit or quietly take it for myself?
27:33.action: Thank God aloud for three specific provisions in your life today, naming Him as the true source of each one.
27:33.prayer: Father, thank You for every good gift that flows through my hands. Keep me humble when things go well, and quick to share what You have given. May my success serve others and honor You. Amen.

27:34.devotion: The lament reaches its tragic center: Tyre sinks into the sea, and all her merchandise and crew go down with her. Everything the city accumulated could not save her in the hour of judgment. Ezekiel's imagery teaches that wealth without humility before God provides no security when trials come.
27:34.reflection: If everything I own suddenly disappeared, what would still be standing in my life?
27:34.action: Take inventory of your treasures today, and choose one way to use a resource you have for someone else's good this week.
27:34.prayer: Lord, so much of what I hold can sink in a moment. Anchor my heart in things that cannot be lost: Your love, Your Word, and Your presence. Make me generous with what is temporary. Amen.

27:35.devotion: News of Tyre's fall ripples outward. Island dwellers stand astonished, and their kings grow afraid, their faces troubled. The collapse of a wealthy power unsettled everyone who depended on it or admired it. Ezekiel shows that earthly securities, when they fail, spread fear far beyond the fallen city itself.
27:35.reflection: Where do I place confidence that would leave me frightened if it collapsed tomorrow?
27:35.action: Name your greatest current worry today, and write beside it one promise of God that speaks to trusting Him in uncertainty.
27:35.prayer: God of steadiness, the shifting powers of this world make people afraid, and I feel that fear too. Ground my heart in Your unchanging reign, so that when systems shake, my peace remains in You. Amen.

27:36.devotion: The lament closes starkly: merchants hiss in scorn, and Tyre becomes a horror, no more forever. In Ezekiel's context this is prophecy of judgment against a proud trading empire, not a promise we may claim against any person or city today. It stands as a sober witness that God opposes pride and defends His righteousness.
27:36.reflection: Do I take pride in things God may one day bring low, and am I willing to be warned by Tyre's example?
27:36.action: Choose one habit of self-promotion today, such as boasting or curating an image, and practice quiet gratitude in its place.
27:36.prayer: Father, Tyre's story warns me that pride ends in loss. Search my heart and expose every boastful place. Give me a humble spirit that finds its worth not in reputation, but in Your grace. Amen.

28:1.devotion: This brief verse marks a transition. Having finished the lament over Tyre as a trading city, Ezekiel receives a new word from the Lord, this time aimed at the city's leader. It reminds us that God speaks specifically into every sphere of life, including the halls of political and economic power.
28:1.reflection: Do I expect God to have something to say about every part of my life, or only the religious parts?
28:1.action: Set aside ten minutes today to listen quietly in prayer before God, inviting Him to speak into an area you have kept off-limits.
28:1.prayer: Lord, Your word came to Your servant again and again, and You still speak today. Give me ears to hear You in every corner of my life, especially the places I have hidden from You. Amen.

28:2.devotion: The prince of Tyre grew so proud of his wealth and coastal fortress that he called himself a god. The Lord's answer is blunt: you are a man, not a god. This is ancient prophecy of judgment on a specific ruler's arrogance, and it exposes a temptation common to every human heart: forgetting that we are creatures, not the Creator.
28:2.reflection: In what subtle ways do I live as though I am the one in charge of my own life?
28:2.action: Practice one deliberate act of humility today, such as admitting a mistake, asking for help, or submitting a plan to God in prayer first.
28:2.prayer: Father, forgive me for the times I have seated myself on a throne that belongs only to You. Remind me daily that I am Your creature and Your child, dependent on Your wisdom and mercy. In Jesus' name, Amen.

28:3.devotion: The Lord quotes, with irony, what Tyre's prince might claim: that he is wiser than Daniel and that no secret is hidden from him. Daniel, a faithful exile known for God-given insight, is the true standard. The verse contrasts self-flattering pride with wisdom that genuinely comes from God alone.
28:3.reflection: Do I seek wisdom from God, or do I trust my own cleverness and call it insight?
28:3.action: Before making one decision today, pause and ask God for wisdom, and consider His Word before you act.
28:3.prayer: Lord, You are the source of all true wisdom, and no secret is hidden from Your sight. Keep me from the flattery of my own thoughts. Make me humble enough to seek Your counsel before I speak or act. Amen.

28:4.devotion: God speaks through Ezekiel against the prince of Tyre, a wealthy trading ruler. His business skill was real: he gained riches and filled treasuries with gold and silver. Yet the passage exposes the danger of attributing success entirely to our own cleverness rather than humbly acknowledging God's provision.
28:4.reflection: When I look at what I have earned or achieved, whose name do I quietly credit first?
28:4.action: List three blessings or successes in your life today, and thank God for each one by name in prayer.
28:4.prayer: Father, forgive me for the times I have praised my own wisdom for what You provided. Every good gift comes from You. Teach me to hold success with open hands and a grateful heart. In Jesus' name, Amen.

28:5.devotion: Tyre's ruler grew richer through skillful trade, but verse five names the real problem: his heart was lifted up because of his riches. Prosperity itself was not condemned; pride produced by prosperity was. Success quietly became the ground of his self-importance.
28:5.reflection: Has something I own or accomplished made me feel superior to others who have less?
28:5.action: Perform one quiet act of generosity today without mentioning it to anyone.
28:5.prayer: Lord, guard my heart when things go well for me. Keep success from swelling my pride or shrinking my compassion. Make me humble in abundance as I would be in need. Through Christ I pray, Amen.

28:6.devotion: Because Tyre's prince set his heart as the heart of a god, God's word of judgment follows. This ruler claimed a position that belongs to the Lord alone. Scripture consistently warns that idolizing ourselves, whether wealth, power, or image, invites God's opposition.
28:6.reflection: In what area of my life am I functioning as if I were the final authority over right and wrong?
28:6.action: Identify one decision you have been avoiding God's input on, and pray about it before acting.
28:6.prayer: Almighty God, You alone are God, and I am not. Forgive the pride that quietly enthrones my own preferences. Help me submit my plans, money, and ambitions to Your lordship today. In Jesus' name, Amen.

28:7.devotion: This is an ancient prophetic announcement of national judgment: God says strangers, fearsome warriors of that era, will come against Tyre. Their swords will expose that the ruler's celebrated wisdom cannot save him. It is descriptive prophecy about a historical event, not a model for believers' conduct today.
28:7.reflection: When pressure or threat comes into my life, do I run first to my own resources or to God?
28:7.action: Name one worry you have been managing alone, and pray it over to God today.
28:7.prayer: Sovereign Lord, You rule over nations and history. When my security is shaken, remind me that no earthly strength or cleverness can replace trust in You. Be my refuge and my steady hope. Amen.

28:8.devotion: Ezekiel continues the solemn prophecy of Tyre's downfall: the proud ruler will be brought low, dying the death of the slain in the seas. The imagery stresses total collapse of status and power. God's judgments on nations in biblical history remind us He takes human pride seriously.
28:8.reflection: What would it mean for me to live today mindful that every position I hold is temporary?
28:8.action: Write down one status, title, or possession you rely on, and pray a sentence surrendering it to God.
28:8.prayer: Eternal God, all human glory fades, but Your word stands forever. Keep me from building my identity on things that pass away. Root my life in Your unfailing love and unshakable kingdom. In Jesus' name, Amen.

28:9.devotion: The rhetorical question pierces: will the dying ruler still claim to be a god in the hand of his killer? God answers plainly: you shall be a man, not a god. Face to face with mortality, every pretense collapses. Only the Lord is divine; humans must live within that truth.
28:9.reflection: What illusions about my own strength would hardship or weakness quickly expose?
28:9.action: Practice one honest acknowledgment of limitation today, asking for help instead of pretending self-sufficiency.
28:9.prayer: Father, I am a creature, and You are Creator. Strip away my illusions of invincibility and teach me humble dependence. Thank You that Your strength meets me honestly in my weakness. Through Christ, Amen.

28:10.devotion: The oracle closes with God's decisive verdict: the prince of Tyre will fall by foreign hands, for the Lord Himself has spoken. The phrase underscores that this is divine judgment, certainly accomplished. God's declarations are not idle warnings; His word carries the authority of reality itself.
28:10.reflection: Do I treat God's warnings in Scripture as seriously as His promises?
28:10.action: Read one passage of Scripture today asking what it asks of you, not only what it offers you.
28:10.prayer: Lord God, Your word is true, both its comfort and its warning. Soften my heart so I do not hear Your cautions and ignore them. Form in me a responsive, obedient spirit today. In Jesus' name, Amen.

28:11.devotion: After the word against the prince of Tyre, the Lord speaks again to Ezekiel. This quiet verse reminds us that prophecy came through ongoing, repeated communion with God. Ezekiel kept listening, and further messages followed. Faithful service often looks like simply staying attentive to God's voice over time.
28:11.reflection: Am I making space to hear from God regularly, or only turning to Him in crisis?
28:11.action: Set aside ten minutes today to read Scripture and listen in silence before God.
28:11.prayer: Lord, You spoke to Your servants again and again, and You still speak through Your word. Give me Ezekiel's attentive heart. Help me keep listening, not only when crisis comes, but every day. Amen.

28:12.devotion: God commands Ezekiel to pronounce a lament over the king of Tyre. Though addressed to a proud human ruler, the language portrays someone endowed with extraordinary wisdom, beauty, and perfection. The lament reminds us that even the most impressive gifts come from God and are never grounds for arrogance.
28:12.reflection: Where have I begun to take credit for gifts God gave me?
28:12.action: Write down three abilities or blessings you possess today, and thank God by name for each one.
28:12.prayer: Father, every good thing in me comes from Your hand. Keep me from pride in my talents and appearance. Teach me to hold Your gifts with gratitude and humility, using them to serve others today. In Jesus' name, Amen.

28:13.devotion: The lament continues with imagery of Eden, describing the ruler adorned with precious stones and created with splendor. Such rich pictures emphasize how glorious a beginning can precede a tragic fall. Beauty and privilege, apart from obedience to God, cannot protect a heart from corruption.
28:13.reflection: Am I valuing my standing with God more than outward signs of success?
28:13.action: Spend five minutes today recalling God's original goodness to you, and jot down memories of His early kindness in your life.
28:13.prayer: Lord, You made all things beautiful, including me. Thank You for every season of blessing You have given. Help me never to trade fellowship with You for treasures that fade. Keep my heart anchored in Your presence. Amen.

28:14.devotion: The figure in the lament is described as an anointed guardian cherub, established by God on His holy mountain. This exalted language underscores intimate nearness to God's presence. Ezekiel's audience heard that even the closest access to holy things offers no security when pride takes root.
28:14.reflection: Do I treat my nearness to God as a privilege or as an entitlement?
28:14.action: Attend a worship service or spend quiet time in God's presence today, consciously approaching Him with reverence rather than routine.
28:14.prayer: Holy God, what a mercy it is to be welcomed near You. Guard me from treating Your presence casually or proudly. Let every moment of closeness to You deepen my reverence, gratitude, and obedience. In Jesus' name, Amen.

28:15.devotion: This verse states that the subject was blameless from creation until iniquity was found in him. The tragic turning point is stark and simple: perfection gave way to sin. It warns every believer that a strong spiritual beginning must be guarded by continued faithfulness and humility.
28:15.reflection: What small compromise could quietly grow into iniquity if I ignore it today?
28:15.action: Identify one habit or attitude you have excused lately, confess it to God, and take one practical step to change it today.
28:15.prayer: Lord, You know how quickly a clean start can turn sour. Search my heart and expose any hidden iniquity before it takes root. Give me grace to walk blamelessly with You today, depending on Your strength. Amen.

28:16.devotion: The lament attributes the fall to abundant trading that filled the heart with violence and sin, resulting in expulsion from God's mountain. In Tyre's context, commercial pride bred corruption and cruelty. The passage warns that greed unchecked eventually drives out reverence, justice, and the presence of God.
28:16.reflection: Has the pursuit of gain begun to crowd out generosity and integrity in my life?
28:16.action: Choose one concrete act of generosity today, such as giving to someone in need or sharing a resource freely.
28:16.prayer: Father, protect me from greed that hardens the heart and harms others. Where ambition has taken too much space in me, uproot it. Make me generous, honest, and just in my work and dealings today. In Jesus' name, Amen.

28:17.devotion: Here the root of the fall is named plainly: pride in beauty corrupted wisdom, and God humbled the proud figure before watching kings. Scripture consistently shows that self-exaltation ends in humiliation. God opposes the proud, and every boast not grounded in Him will finally be brought low.
28:17.reflection: In what area of life am I quietly admiring myself instead of glorifying God?
28:17.action: Practice one deliberate act of humility today, such as accepting correction graciously or crediting someone else publicly.
28:17.prayer: Lord, keep my heart from being lifted up by appearance, achievement, or praise. When pride whispers, remind me of who You are and who I am before You. Clothe me in humility today, for Your glory. Amen.

28:18.devotion: The lament declares that multiplied iniquity and corrupt trading defiled the ruler's sanctuaries, bringing judgment like fire that consumed him. What was meant to be holy became polluted by greed and pride. The verse soberly shows that sin spreads, contaminating even sacred spaces and calling forth God's justice.
28:18.reflection: Is there anything in my life or worship that sin has quietly defiled?
28:18.action: Clean out one physical or spiritual space today, such as your room or prayer life, asking God to purify what has grown careless.
28:18.prayer: Purifying God, burn away everything in me that defiles what should be holy. Forgive the sins that have crept into my worship, work, and relationships. Make my whole life, body, and spirit a clean sanctuary for You. Amen.

28:19.devotion: The lament closes with the nations astonished: the once-admired ruler has become a horror, coming to a final end. Tyre's story stands as a witness that no glory apart from God endures. For God's people, the passage invites trust in His justice rather than envy of worldly splendor.
28:19.reflection: Which worldly glories am I tempted to envy, forgetting they do not last?
28:19.action: Read a short passage about God's eternal kingdom today, and write down one way you will invest in what lasts forever.
28:19.prayer: Eternal God, thank You that Your kingdom outlasts every earthly empire. Free me from envying splendor that fades and from fearing powers that fall. Fix my hope on what is everlasting, and help me live today for You. Amen.

28:20.devotion: This brief verse marks a turning point in Ezekiel's oracles against the nations. After messages concerning Tyre and its prince, the word of the LORD comes again to the prophet. It reminds us that God still speaks, and that His message continues moving from judgment on prideful nations toward hope for His people.
28:20.reflection: Am I making quiet space to listen for God's word to me today?
28:20.action: Set aside ten minutes today to read Scripture slowly and listen before speaking or deciding anything.
28:20.prayer: Lord, thank You that You still speak through Your Word. Quiet my heart, open my ears, and help me receive Your word with humility and obedience today. In Jesus' name, amen.

28:21.devotion: God commands Ezekiel to turn his attention to Sidon, Tyre's ancient neighbor, and to prophesy against her. The phrase 'set your face' signals resolve and seriousness. Prophets were called to deliver hard messages faithfully, even when the word was unwelcome.
28:21.reflection: Would I remain faithful in delivering or living God's truth even when it is unpopular?
28:21.action: Speak one honest, gracious word of biblical truth today where silence would be easier, doing so with kindness.
28:21.prayer: Father, give me courage like Ezekiel's, to face difficult tasks without flinching. Help me speak and live Your truth faithfully, wrapped in love and humility. In Jesus' name, amen.

28:22.devotion: God declares Himself against Sidon, promising that He will be glorified and known as the LORD even through His judgments. In Ezekiel, the refrain 'they shall know that I am the LORD' runs throughout. God's holiness is not mocked; His glory will be recognized, whether in judgment or in mercy.
28:22.reflection: Do my daily choices honor God's holiness, or do I treat His name lightly?
28:22.action: Choose one area of life today—speech, spending, or habits—and align it deliberately with God's holiness.
28:22.prayer: Holy Lord, You alone are God, and Your glory will be known in all the earth. Let my life reflect Your holiness, so that others may see and know You. In Jesus' name, amen.

28:23.devotion: This verse describes coming judgment on Sidon in ancient warfare imagery—pestilence, blood, and the sword. Ezekiel spoke to a violent era when nations faced conquest. The purpose is stated clearly: 'Then they shall know that I am the LORD.' God's judgments exposed false securities and called people to acknowledge Him.
28:23.reflection: What false security am I relying on instead of trusting the Lord?
28:23.action: Identify one false source of security you lean on, and take a step today to trust God in that area instead.
28:23.prayer: Sovereign God, You see every nation and every heart. Strip away my false securities and teach me to rest in You alone, the Lord who judges justly. In Jesus' name, amen.

28:24.devotion: God promises that Israel will no longer suffer from hostile neighbors like a 'pricking brier' or 'painful thorn.' The imagery acknowledges the real pain of living among those who despised God's people. The outcome, again, is recognition: all will know that He is the Lord GOD who defends His people.
28:24.reflection: Where am I experiencing 'thorns' of hostility or hardship, and am I bringing them to God?
28:24.action: Name one ongoing frustration or hostile relationship to God in prayer today, entrusting it to Him rather than harboring bitterness.
28:24.prayer: Father, You know the thorns that prick me—people and pressures that wear me down. I entrust them to You, the God who sees, defends, and makes all things known. In Jesus' name, amen.

28:25.devotion: Here the tone turns to promise. God pledges to gather Israel from exile among the nations and to be shown holy in them before the Gentiles. The land He swore to Jacob would again be home. Judgment on the nations serves a larger purpose: the restoration of God's scattered people for His glory.
28:25.reflection: Do I believe God can gather and restore what feels scattered and broken in my life?
28:25.action: Write down one broken or scattered area of your life and pray over it daily this week, asking God to restore it.
28:25.prayer: Faithful God, You gather the scattered and keep Your promises. Restore what is broken in me and around me, and let my restored life point others to Your glory. In Jesus' name, amen.

28:26.devotion: The promise continues with a picture of ordinary peace: dwelling safely, building houses, planting vineyards. After exile and threat, God envisions a restored life of quiet, productive normalcy. Security comes not from walls or armies but from the Lord executing justice, so that all will know He is their God.
28:26.reflection: Am I thanking God for the ordinary gifts of safety, home, and daily provision?
28:26.action: Tend something growing today—water a plant, prepare a nourishing meal, or tend your home—as an act of gratitude to God.
28:26.prayer: Lord of restoration, thank You for ordinary mercies: a place to live, food to eat, work to do. Teach me to dwell securely in You and to notice Your daily care. In Jesus' name, amen.

29:1.devotion: This verse begins a new section with a precise date—the tenth year, tenth month, twelfth day—placing Ezekiel's oracle against Egypt within real history, near Jerusalem's siege. The dating reminds us that God speaks into actual events and times, not vague abstraction. His word addresses real nations, real crises, and real people.
29:1.reflection: Do I trust that God's Word speaks meaningfully into my actual, dated, everyday circumstances?
29:1.action: Journal today's date alongside one current concern, inviting God's Word to speak into that specific situation this week.
29:1.prayer: Timeless God, You spoke into real days and real troubles through Your prophets. Speak into my concrete circumstances today, and anchor my trust in Your Word. In Jesus' name, amen.

29:2.devotion: God commissions Ezekiel to confront Pharaoh, the ruler of a powerful nation that Israel was tempted to trust. Setting his face against Egypt means delivering an unwelcome message faithfully. God's word speaks even to empires, not only to individuals, and His prophets must not soften what He commands.
29:2.reflection: When God calls me to speak or live truthfully, am I willing to face powerful people or popular opinion?
29:2.action: Identify one truth you have been avoiding saying or living out, and take one respectful step toward faithfulness today.
29:2.prayer: Lord, give me courage like Ezekiel's, to stand firm in Your truth even when it is unpopular. Help me speak with humility and love, trusting that Your word is stronger than any human power. Amen.

29:3.devotion: Pharaoh is pictured as a great creature lounging in the Nile, boasting that he made the river himself. Egypt's pride in its life-giving river became a claim of self-made divinity. God opposes those who take credit for what only He provides and who exalt themselves above Him.
29:3.reflection: Where in my life am I tempted to say, like Pharaoh, that what I have is my own achievement?
29:3.action: Write down three blessings you tend to call your own, and thank God for each one specifically today.
29:3.prayer: Father, forgive me for the times I have claimed credit for what You have given. You are the source of every good thing. Teach me to hold my gifts with gratitude and humility before You. Amen.

29:4.devotion: God promises to drag the proud ruler from his river like a hooked crocodile, with all he caught clinging to him. The image shows that no power or position can resist God's pull. What Pharaoh considered secure, God can overturn by a single act of judgment.
29:4.reflection: What comfort or achievement am I clinging to as if it could never be taken from me?
29:4.action: Hold one possession or plan loosely today by offering it to God in prayer and asking Him to direct its use.
29:4.prayer: Lord, remind me that every security I hold rests in Your hands, not mine. Loose my grip on things that cannot last, and anchor my heart in You alone. Amen.

29:5.devotion: The prophecy declares that Pharaoh and his allies will be left unburied in the open field, given to beasts and birds. In ancient culture, an unburied body was a mark of shame and defeat. God warns that pride ends in loss, and His judgment strips away every false refuge.
29:5.reflection: If everything I boast about were stripped away, what would remain of my life before God?
29:5.action: Spend five minutes today reflecting on what you want to remain at the end of your life, and note one step toward it.
29:5.prayer: God of justice, keep me from building a life on pride that ends in emptiness. Root me instead in what lasts: faith, love, and obedience to You. Amen.

29:6.devotion: God says Egypt's fall will teach its people that He is the LORD, because Egypt proved to be a fragile staff of reed for Israel. Rather than bearing weight, the reed splintered. God exposes unreliable supports so that His people learn to depend on Him, not on unstable alliances.
29:6.reflection: Whose strength am I leaning on instead of God's, and has it ever let me down?
29:6.action: Name one support you lean on besides God, and pray over it today, surrendering your trust to Him first.
29:6.prayer: Father, You alone are a dependable support. Forgive me for leaning on things that splinter under pressure. Teach me to bring my whole weight to You first, trusting Your unfailing strength. Amen.

29:7.devotion: The reed image continues: when Israel grasped Egypt, it broke and tore their shoulders; when they leaned on it, their backs trembled. Trusting Egypt brought injury, not help. This is a sober picture of misplaced reliance, reminding God's people that false supports wound those who depend on them.
29:7.reflection: Has relying on a person, habit, or plan for what only God provides ever left me hurt or shaken?
29:7.action: Choose one unhealthy reliance today and replace one moment of turning to it with a moment of prayer instead.
29:7.prayer: Lord, heal the wounds caused by the broken reeds I have leaned on. Keep me from misplaced trust, and let me find in You a support that never fails or injures. Amen.

29:8.devotion: Because of Egypt's failure and pride, God announces that a sword will come upon the nation, striking both people and livestock. This is ancient covenant judgment language, describing consequences for a nation that exalted itself and proved faithless. The passage warns that God does not ignore arrogance or betrayal indefinitely.
29:8.reflection: How do I respond when I see pride and injustice go unaddressed—do I trust God's timing and justice?
29:8.action: When you notice pride or injustice today, respond with honest prayer for God's justice rather than despair or cynicism.
29:8.prayer: Righteous God, You see every pride and betrayal, and nothing escapes Your notice. Help me trust Your justice without despairing, and keep my own heart humble before You. Amen.

29:9.devotion: The chapter returns to the root issue: Pharaoh declared, "The River is mine, and I have made it." God answers that desolation will come, and through it Egypt will know that He is the LORD. Even judgment serves God's larger purpose of revealing Himself as the true Maker and Sovereign over all nations.
29:9.reflection: Do my daily choices reflect a genuine belief that God is the Maker and Owner of all I have?
29:9.action: End today by acknowledging God as owner of your time, money, and abilities, and plan tomorrow around that truth.
29:9.prayer: Sovereign Lord, You made all things, and all things belong to You. Deliver me from the illusion of self-made security. Let my life declare that You are the LORD, Creator and Sustainer of everything. Amen.

29:10.devotion: In this oracle, God speaks against Egypt and its life-giving Nile streams, promising judgment stretching across the whole land, from its northern edges to its southern border. Egypt had trusted in its river and its power. The passage reminds us that no nation, river, or resource stands beyond God's sovereign authority.
29:10.reflection: Where am I quietly trusting in worldly security more than in God?
29:10.action: Identify one source of security you lean on besides God, and spend five minutes today praying about that dependence.
29:10.prayer: Lord God, You rule over every nation and every river. Forgive me when I place my confidence in things that cannot save. Teach me to rest in You alone, the true source of every good thing. Amen.

29:11.devotion: God declares that Egypt will become so desolate that neither people nor animals will pass through, and it will lie uninhabited forty years. This is ancient prophetic judgment imagery, spoken to a proud empire. It underscores God's seriousness about humbling powers that set themselves up as secure and self-sufficient.
29:11.reflection: How do I respond when God's warnings confront my pride or complacency?
29:11.action: Read this passage slowly, then write down one warning or conviction God seems to be speaking into your life right now.
29:11.prayer: Father, Your word is weighty and true. Soften my heart when Your warnings come. Keep me from hardening myself against Your voice, and lead me to humility and repentance today. In Jesus' name, Amen.

29:12.devotion: God announces that Egypt will be made desolate like other devastated lands, its cities laid waste, and its people scattered among the nations for forty years. The verse portrays complete displacement and loss. It reminds readers that God's judgments are thorough, yet they unfold within His larger purposes for the nations.
29:12.reflection: What would remain standing in my life if God stripped away every false support?
